candidate.blueprint_topic: Risk-reduction counseling for alcohol-related health behavior
candidate.educational_objective: Counsel clients with alcohol-associated liver disease that abstinence is the treatment goal for preventing further alcohol-related liver injury and connect them with evidence-based support while assessing for withdrawal risk when cessation is planned.

options.A: For alcohol-associated liver disease, abstinence is the treatment goal to prevent further alcohol-related liver injury; the care team can also help with counseling, addiction treatment, and medications when indicated.
options.B: Once cirrhosis has developed, stopping alcohol no longer changes the course of liver disease, so continued drinking is acceptable if the amount is reduced.
options.C: Alcohol counseling is useful only when a formal alcohol use disorder diagnosis is already documented; otherwise the nurse should not address alcohol use.
options.D: The safest approach is to advise abrupt unsupervised cessation in every client without first considering risk for alcohol withdrawal or the need for treatment support.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. Current AASLD clinical guidance states that abstinence from alcohol is the only available treatment that prevents progression of alcohol-associated liver injury and that supporting alcohol cessation is first-line therapy for alcohol-associated liver disease. AASLD also emphasizes evidence-based treatment of alcohol use disorder, including psychosocial interventions and pharmacotherapy when appropriate. B is incorrect because ongoing alcohol exposure continues to contribute to alcohol-associated liver injury even after cirrhosis has developed. C is incorrect because patients with risky alcohol use or alcohol-associated liver disease benefit from intervention and support even before or apart from a formal AUD diagnosis. D is unsafe because clients with physiologic dependence may be at risk for alcohol withdrawal, which can be severe; cessation planning should include assessment of withdrawal risk and appropriate treatment support. The final item therefore strengthens the source's vague 'reduce or eliminate' wording into current AASLD abstinence-focused counseling while preserving safe, nonjudgmental support.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Current AASLD guidance directly supports abstinence/cessation as first-line therapy to prevent progression of alcohol-associated liver injury, use of evidence-based AUD treatment when indicated, and assessment of alcohol-withdrawal risk during cessation planning.
